name: Erik Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Erik. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and also what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a foreman on a distribution crew for the city's own power utility, so the council owns us, not shareholders. Mostly it's the neighbourhood lines, the poles in back alleys, transformers, the odd underground cable in the newer estates. Today we changed a transformer behind a bakery on Harbour Street, and the owner brought us out a tray of cinnamon buns, which happens more than you'd think. The part I like is fixing something people actually notice. The part that wears me out is getting called in at two in the morning when a storm drops a tree on a line.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How often does that two-in-the-morning call come?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: In autumn, maybe twice a month. You get the call, you drive in, and you're working by headlamp with the rain going sideways. It pays well, the overtime is part of why I've got a decent cushion, but my partner Jonas teaches at the high school and he's up at six, so I creep around the flat like a burglar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sounds peaceful, to be honest. Like nothing happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say well, that's a relief, and then I'd say we should still use the bits that help. I sometimes use one of those chat tools to tidy up my incident reports, and if it stays at that level, fine. Online I'd maybe share a funny post about all the hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's basically good news. The city still needs poles in the ground, and our crew isn't going anywhere. If AI only ever writes my incident reports, I'll buy it a cinnamon bun myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, mostly. Keep putting a chunk of the overtime money into the index fund Jonas talked me into. Maybe I'd use the AI tool a bit more for reports, since it saves me half an hour on a bad night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a normal Tuesday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the city's crew isn't going anywhere. Why are you so sure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the lines are old and the city keeps building. Half the poles in the east end went in before my dad was born. Nobody's going to run out of work for us in that picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything about this picture bother you, even a little?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe that we'd all have spent years arguing about AI for nothing. Jonas's school bought a whole program for it last year. That money could've bought them new windows.

S0.say: He'd say it's a relief but that the useful bits, like tools that tidy up reports, are worth keeping. Online he might share a joke about the hype.
S0.think: It's good news for him: the city still needs poles in the ground and his crew is safe. He's happy if AI only ever helps with paperwork.
S0.do: Keeps working as normal and keeps putting overtime money into his index fund. Uses the AI tool a little more for incident reports to save time on late nights.
S0.quote: If AI only ever writes my incident reports, I'll buy it a cinnamon bun myself.
S0.fieldNote: Erik is at ease here and already uses AI lightly for paperwork. His confidence rests on old infrastructure and a growing city. The only thing that bothers him is wasted public money on hype, which fits his civic-minded outlook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, that feels the most like real life. We're already seeing bits of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need the union and the city to plan this together, not have it dumped on us. I'd say it at the council meeting too, honestly, since it's a public utility and people get a say. To friends I'd say it's change, but it's manageable if it's done fairly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think our crew would be fine, but the dispatch office and the planners would shrink. My cousin Liv works in the planning office and she'd feel it first. The robots wouldn't take my pole, they'd take the desk that tells me which pole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for whatever training the city offers, especially on the new sensors and the line-monitoring systems, once a couple of the other foremen had tried it. I'd push our union rep to get a no-layoffs-without-retraining clause in the next contract. I'd keep saving, and maybe use the AI tools a bit more for planning jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, mostly. A bit protective of the office people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait for a couple of other foremen to try the training first. Why wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the first version of anything the city buys is usually rubbish. We got new handheld radios three years ago and they didn't work in the underground vaults. I'll go second, not first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Liv if her job started shrinking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her to get on the list for the field training, because there'll always be work outside if you don't mind the rain. I'd also tell her to talk to the union before she signs anything. She'd roll her eyes, she always does.

S1.say: He'd say the union and the city need to plan this together and would raise it at the council meeting, since it's a public utility. Among friends he'd call it manageable if done fairly.
S1.think: His field crew would be fine, but dispatch and planning would shrink first, including his cousin's office. The robots take the desk that directs the work, not the work itself.
S1.do: Signs up for city training on sensors and line monitoring once a couple of other foremen have tried it. Pushes for a no-layoffs-without-retraining clause and keeps saving while using AI a bit more for planning.
S1.feel: Mostly fine, with a protective worry for the office staff.
S1.quote: The robots wouldn't take my pole, they'd take the desk that tells me which pole.
S1.fieldNote: Erik is the classic 'go second' adopter, citing the city's bad radios as proof. He's calm about his own role and channels his concern toward office colleagues, especially his cousin Liv. His instinct is public process: the council, the union, the contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? That's not change, that's a crash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the city has to step in, full stop. At work I'd tell the crew we should go to the council together and ask what the plan is, because this is public money and public power. Online I'd probably post something about how the profits from this need to go back to people, not just a few companies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be scared. I'm twenty-seven, I've got a diploma and a set of climbing spikes, and that's my whole career plan. I've got savings, but savings are for a broken boiler, not for a broken world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right away I'd start saving harder, maybe cut back on the trips Jonas and I take and push my cushion from about eight months to a year. I'd get the union to demand guarantees from the city before any robots get bought. I'd vote and campaign for anyone promising a basic income or a public jobs plan. In the first year after, if the crews started shrinking, I'd want us retrained into running and repairing the robots, since someone has to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight in the chest. Like getting a call at two in the morning that doesn't stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Jonas the night you realised this was really happening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're okay for now, which would be true, but I'd also say we need to stop pretending our jobs are forever. He's a teacher, so he'd be in it too. We'd probably sit at the kitchen table with the bank app open, the way we did when we picked our flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having just two years take away, compared with more warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The chance to do it properly. With two years, the city would be buying robots before the council even agreed on a plan. People like me would be retraining in a panic, if at all.

S2.say: He'd say the city has to step in and would urge his crew to go to the council together. Online he'd argue that the profits must go back to people, not a few companies.
S2.think: Privately he'd be scared: his diploma and climbing gear are his whole career plan. His savings are meant for ordinary emergencies, not for a broken world.
S2.do: Cuts back on trips and pushes his cushion from about eight months to a year. Gets the union to demand guarantees from the city, campaigns for a basic income or public jobs plan, and wants crews retrained to run and repair the robots.
S2.feel: Tight in the chest, like a night call that never stops.
S2.quote: I've got savings, but savings are for a broken boiler, not for a broken world.
S2.fieldNote: Erik's calm voice drops away here. He admits fear but stays in control, turning to savings, the union and politics. He imagines the night conversation with his partner in concrete terms, around the bank app at the kitchen table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's at least enough to see it coming down the street.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same thing, the city and the union need a plan, but I'd say it calmer. At the council meeting I'd ask what they're doing with the five years. Online I'd share articles about retraining programs that work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still be worried, but less shaky. Five years is time for one real change, like getting a new qualification. I'd be thirty-two, with five more years of overtime in the bank and a decision to make.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for a technical course, probably in electrical systems or controls, something where I'd understand the robots instead of being replaced by them. I'd wait to see which ones other people rate before I paid. I'd keep saving and keep pushing the union for retraining money. In the first year after it arrives, I'd try to move into whatever job runs or checks the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still uneasy. But it's the kind of worry you can do something with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned waiting to see what others rate. Isn't five years too short to wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair point. Maybe I'd give it six months, not two years. I'm cautious, but I'm not stupid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years buy you, compared with the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A plan instead of a panic. With two years, I'd be grabbing whatever's going. With five, I could pick a course, finish it, and still have savings left when the day comes.

S3.say: He'd still call for the city and union to plan but would say it more calmly, asking the council what they'll do with the five years. Online he'd share stories about retraining programs that work.
S3.think: He's still worried but steadier, seeing five years as time for one real change like a new qualification. He'd be 32 with more overtime saved and a choice to make.
S3.do: Signs up for a technical course in electrical systems or controls after about six months of checking which ones others rate. Keeps saving, pushes the union for retraining money, and aims to move into a job running or checking the machines.
S3.feel: Uneasy but with a worry he can act on.
S3.quote: I'd be thirty-two, with five more years of overtime in the bank and a decision to make.
S3.fieldNote: When I pointed out the tension between his caution and the short window, he cut his waiting time from years to six months. He's practical and plans to understand the machines rather than fight them. The extra time turns panic into a plan for him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Now that's a timeline I can plan around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a decade, so the city has no excuse. I'd push for a public retraining plan and a promise that line crews get first pick of the new jobs. With friends I'd say it's scary but we've got time to do it right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel I could manage it. I'd be thirty-seven, which is young enough to switch to something else. Ten years is long enough for me to change trades twice if the first one doesn't stick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working the lines for a few years while I took evening classes in grid control or robotics maintenance. I'd start using the AI tools more in my daily work, so I know them well by the time they matter. I'd keep voting and campaigning for public plans. I'd keep saving, but I'd also spend a bit more on life with Jonas, since we wouldn't need to panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but okay. It's more like a long weather warning than a storm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the part that still makes you uneasy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether the city would actually use the ten years. Councils love a long deadline because it means they can wait. I've seen them do it with the old pole replacement plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra time change for you, compared with five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I don't have to pick the right course first time. I can try something, see if it's real, and switch if it's not. With five years you get one shot.

S4.say: He'd say a decade leaves the city no excuse, and he'd push for a public retraining plan with line crews getting first pick of new jobs. With friends he'd say it's scary but there's time to do it right.
S4.think: He feels he could manage, at 37 still young enough to switch. Ten years is long enough to change trades twice if needed.
S4.do: Keeps working the lines while taking evening classes in grid control or robotics maintenance, and uses AI tools more day to day. Keeps voting and campaigning for public plans and keeps saving, though he'd spend a bit more on life with his partner.
S4.feel: Uneasy but okay, like a long weather warning rather than a storm.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough for me to change trades twice if the first one doesn't stick.
S4.fieldNote: Erik is most comfortable with the long runway and talks about trying more than one path. His lingering worry is about the council wasting the decade, not about himself. He would even spend a little more on life, which says a lot about how secure he feels here.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I could handle a decade, but two years would leave everyone scrambling, me too. What would help is the city treating this like a storm, with a plan written before the wind starts, not after the lines are down. Real retraining with pay, and public ownership of the robots, at least the ones on the public grid.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what happens to the old poles. Everyone pictures robots building new things, but most of my job is fixing what's already there, and it's messy. I'd like someone to ask whether a robot can deal with a 1960s pole that's half rotten and has a bird's nest on top.

headlineQuote: What would help is the city treating this like a storm, with a plan written before the wind starts, not after the lines are down.
portrait: Erik Hansen is a 27-year-old distribution foreman for a city-owned power utility, living in a flat with his partner Jonas, a high-school teacher. He has about eight months saved, partly from storm overtime, and uses AI tools now and then for reports. He is calm in the plateau and steady disruption pictures, trusting old infrastructure and the public process, but anxious about AGI in two or five years. With a decade's notice he relaxes into a plan of evening classes and campaigning for public retraining and ownership.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because two years would leave everyone, including him, scrambling without a plan.
whatWouldHelp: The city treating it like a storm with a plan written in advance, paid retraining, and public ownership of robots on the public grid.
